pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: so that he might not seem to present the opposite) to it, that is, eloquence, he says: 'and my preaching (was) not in persuasive words of wisdom', since there is a wisdom not of phrases but of divine knowledge, of Spirit and power. For since the Holy Spirit both supplies a word of wisdom and also works wonders, he said 'in demonstration of Spirit and power': for what is said is not yet a demonstration, but the wonder has the demonstration. [Second column, page 231, parallel to the 2:3-4 note:] He shows that he did not preach trusting in any human might either; for he was in weakness and fear and trembling and in such things, as being in persecutions and afflictions. [Label 1 Cor 2:5.] For since by only speaking he would differ in nothing from those using wisdom and trusting their own word, but by doing powers he showed the strength of God, and from there the preaching (had its force), well he added: 'but in demonstration of Spirit and power, so that your faith may not be in wisdom of man but in power of God'. [Label 1 Cor 2:6.] That is, not among the learned, but among those perfect according to godliness. And he said 'among the perfect', not however 'to the perfect', because the one who speaks to chance persons often also receives contradiction, but the one who introduces the saving word to the perfect and godly does not (merely) speak, as depositing and storing up the words in their souls. [Label 1 Cor 2:7-8.] If it had been hidden, clearly finding it was not (a matter) of reasonings, but truly revealing (it) was God's. And the proof of not understanding (stands) instead of saying (so): 'for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory'. He calls rulers those around Pilate and Herod, and Lord of glory the God made flesh. [Label 1 Cor 2:9.] This quotation is not carried in the Old (Testament) in these phrases, but in other words signifying the same: for Isaiah says 'Lord, who believed our hearing? and the arm of the Lord, to whom was it revealed?' (Isa 53:1) 'and his generation who will tell?' (Isa 53:8), and Moses: 'the hidden things to the Lord God' (Deut 29:28 LXX = 29:29). And the hidden (thing) of God clearly escaped both eye and heart. One must not however think that without judgement God revealed the mystery to some, and let others perish in ignorance, but one must know and be persuaded that by his foreknowing power he provided to each, having measured what is according to worth toward (their) benefit; for he foresees the choice of each even before he comes to be. [Label 1 Cor 2:10.] He called depths of God his deepest dispensations that escape us. Through these he shows that it (the Spirit) searches, not as being ignorant but as knowing. And since some say that now the Father is called Spirit, others the Son, one must speak toward both. The Father then cannot be meant: for he says 'but we received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit which is from God' (1 Cor 2:12), and no one is from himself; for if it were said of God, from whom (is) God? The Son it is possible to suspect, but that he is the one about whom the passage (speaks) is not possible: for who would say God the Word searches in order to learn the things of God? And if they should say the Son is taught, how did they not see from the following that as a man's spirit knows the things in him, so also the Spirit of God? Apart from this, throughout the whole passage the Holy Spirit is shown. One must observe that he says the Holy Spirit is from God, but the unclean (spirit) he did not say (is) from the world, but of the world; for the Paraclete is not a part of God, but the devil (is) as a part of creation according to having come to be. And the Holy Spirit (is) from God. [Label 1 Cor 2:11-13.] Not in order to show that, as in us our spirit (is) better than us, so also in God the Spirit (is) better than him, (when) immediately saying 'for who of men knows the things of the man except the spirit in him?' But what (of) 'in' (and) 'of God'? For 'in him' (is) a part completing the whole man, but 'from him' shows the cause. One must observe that God and the Holy Spirit (are) two persons, but man and the spirit in him (are) not two persons but one man. So showing the exact identity of Father and Spirit in knowledge, he compared the knowledge of the spirit in us to the knowledge of Father and Spirit, so that it might be shown that, as in us in the one and the same spirit, that is in the soul and the mind, there is no discord of union, but we know what we know, so also in Father and Holy Spirit there is no discord of knowledge but identity. 'That we may know the things granted to us by God': the Spirit having given, the mind having grasped. 'Which we also speak.' Again he shows another (thing): not only, he says, not (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …to it, eloquence, he says, "and my preaching was not in persuasive words of wisdom." For there is a wisdom that is not a matter of phrases but of divine knowledge, of the Spirit and of power. The Holy Spirit both supplies a word of wisdom and works wonders, and so he said, "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." What is said is not yet proof; a wonder carries its proof with it.
The second catena form adds: He shows that he did not preach relying on any human power either.

On 1 Corinthians 2:5: Had he only spoken, he would have been no different from those who use wisdom and trust in their own speech. But by working mighty deeds he showed the strength of God, and the preaching drew its force from there. So he rightly went on, "but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God."

On 1 Corinthians 2:6: That is, not among the learned, but among those who are mature in godliness. He said "among the mature," not "to the mature." Someone who talks to whoever happens along often meets contradiction too. But someone who brings the saving word to the mature and godly does not simply talk: he lays the words up in their souls and stores them there like treasure.

On 1 Corinthians 2:7–8: If it had been hidden, then clearly finding it out was not a task for reasoning; revealing it truly belonged to God. In place of saying that they did not understand, he gives the proof of it: "for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." By "rulers" he means Pilate and Herod and those around them, and by "the Lord of glory" God made flesh.

On 1 Corinthians 2:9: This quotation is not found in the Old Testament in these words, but in other words with the same meaning. Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" (Isaiah 53:1) and, "Who shall tell of his generation?" (Isaiah 53:8). And Moses says, "The hidden things belong to the Lord God" (Deuteronomy 29:29). What is hidden with God plainly escaped both eye and heart. We must not think, however, that God revealed the mystery to some without discernment and let others perish in ignorance. We must know, and be convinced, that by his power of foreknowledge he measured out to each what each deserved, for each one's good, and gave it. For he foresees each person's choice even before that person exists.

On 1 Corinthians 2:10: By "the depths of God" he means God's deepest dispensations, which escape our notice. By these words he shows that the Spirit searches, not as one who does not know, but as one who knows. Some say that "Spirit" here means the Father, others the Son, so we must answer both. It cannot mean the Father, for he says, "We have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God" (1 Corinthians 2:12), and no one is from himself; if it were said of God, from whom would God be? One might suspect it means the Son, but he cannot be the one the passage is about. Who would say that God the Word searches in order to learn the things of God? And if they were to say that the Son is taught, how did they fail to see from what follows that the Spirit of God knows as a man's spirit knows what is in him? Besides, the whole passage shows that the Holy Spirit is meant. Notice too that he says the Holy Spirit is "from God," but he did not say the unclean spirit is "from the world," only "of the world." The Paraclete is not a part of God, but the devil, since he came into being, is a part of creation. The Holy Spirit, then, is from God.

On 1 Corinthians 2:11–13: He does not mean that, as our spirit within us is better than we are, so the Spirit in God is better than God, when he says straight away, "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him?" Then what of "in," and of "from God"? "In him" points to a part that fills out the whole man, while "from him" points to the cause. Note too that God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, while a man and the spirit in him are not two persons but one man. So, to show that the Father and the Spirit are exactly the same in knowledge, he compared the knowledge of the spirit in us with the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit. As in us there is no discord within the one and the same spirit, that is, the soul and the mind, and we know what we know, so in the Father and the Holy Spirit there is no discord of knowledge, but sameness. "That we might know the things freely given to us by God": the Spirit gave them, and the mind took hold of them. "Which we also speak." Again he shows something more: not only, he says, not…

choices.why: Second-column form of the 2:3-4 note (persecutions, weakness, fear and trembling) already translated in u01-rem-mid; only 'he did not preach relying on any human power' has no counterpart.
rejected: printing the whole second form again

choices.why: λαλεῖ is contrasted with laying up words in the soul; 'simply' makes the contrast audible without adding a claim.
rejected: does not speak (reads as a contradiction)

choices.why: Read as reflexive (αὑτοῦ); the next clause ('from whom would God be?') requires it.
rejected: no one of it is [the Father] (old English)

choices.term: ἀλλὰ τί τὸ ἐν τοῦ θεοῦ;
choices.english: Then what of 'in,' and of 'from God'?
choices.why: The question is compressed in the Greek; the answer contrasts 'in him' with 'from him', so the English keeps both words without adding an argument.
